goal.title: Goal and requirements
goal.why: NASA starts every mission from the end product and turns it into measurable requirements; every later decision is checked against them.
goal.sources: Mass margin: GSFC-STD-1000 Gold Rules, Table 1.06-1 (Pre-Phase A).
goal.conflict: Resources are shared, so the roles pull in different directions — there is no single perfect design.

roles.planner: Orbit, launcher and ground stations. Answers for budget, comms and schedule.
roles.scientist: Instruments. Answers for the data that reaches Earth.
roles.engineer: Solar arrays, battery, radio, computer, attitude control and engine. Answers for power.
roles.designer: The bus, which side each part faces and the mass margin. Answers for mass and the fit in the fairing.

concept.hint: A higher orbit lasts longer and stations see the spacecraft for longer, but the signal is weaker and launchers lift less mass there.
concept.hintIss: The ship goes into a low orbit in the station's plane, waits until the ISS is the right angle ahead, then climbs with two engine burns (Hohmann transfer).

physics.orbit: One orbit takes {{periodMin}} min at {{speedKmS}} km/s: the higher the orbit, the slower and longer it is.
physics.eclipse: The Earth's shadow covers {{eclipseFraction}}% of every orbit; the panels give nothing there and the battery carries the load.
physics.power: On average the panels give {{generationW}} W and the spacecraft uses {{consumptionW}} W.
physics.downlink: The stations hear the spacecraft {{minutesPerDay}} min a day — {{gbPerDay}} GB a day reach the Earth.
physics.linkBudget: At {{distanceKm}} km the signal fades with the square of the distance, so the radio really sends {{rateKbps}} kbit/s.
physics.storage: The on-board memory holds {{storageGb}} GB; {{lostGb}} GB did not fit before the next pass and were overwritten.
physics.storage_zero: The on-board memory holds {{storageGb}} GB — enough to keep every byte until the next pass.
physics.drag: Thin air at this height (density {{densityKgM3}} kg/m³) brakes the spacecraft: the orbit sinks {{altitudeLossKmPerYear}} km a year.
physics.rocketEquation: The mission needs Δv {{deltaVms}} m/s; by the rocket equation that burns {{propellantKg}} kg of propellant.
physics.hohmann: Climbing to the station takes two engine burns: {{deltaV1ms}} m/s and {{deltaV2ms}} m/s (Hohmann transfer).
physics.phasing: The ship gains {{degPerOrbit}}° on the station every orbit — {{phasingDays}} days of phasing to catch up.
physics.planeChange: The orbit plane has to turn by {{deltaInclinationDeg}}°, which costs {{deltaVms}} m/s.
physics.earthRotation: The Earth's spin gives {{bonusMs}} m/s for free along the orbit.

tutorial.title: Training
tutorial.allGood: No warnings from the roles — try a cheaper or lighter part and see what changes.

goal.title: Your first CubeSat
goal.do: Read the goal: send 2 GB of measurements in 6 months, spend no more than 150 k and launch by month 12. Then go to Concept.
goal.why: Every NASA mission starts here: first what is needed, then the hardware. Later every choice is checked against these numbers.

concept.title: Where it will fly
concept.do: The orbit is fixed: astronauts release your CubeSat from the ISS at 415 km. Pick a ground station that can hear your radio.
concept.why: At 415 km there is still a little air. It brakes the satellite, so it lives months, not decades — enough for a 6-month mission.

design.title: Build the satellite
design.do: Start from the ready-made set, then change one part at a time: panels, battery, radio. Watch the six bars at the top and the role comments.
design.why: Every part costs mass, power and money. A green bar has a margin; a red one means a limit is broken.

flight.title: Watch it fly
flight.do: Press play. Watch the orbit altitude and the data delivered against the goal line.
flight.why: Without an engine the CubeSat slowly sinks because air drags on it. Data reaches the Earth only while it flies over a station.

report.title: What happened and why
report.do: Read the bottleneck first, then the chain of the segment that failed. Go back to any stage, change one thing and fly again.
report.why: Engineers learn the same way: every attempt is compared with the previous one.

cubesat.name: CubeSat
cubesat.text: A small satellite built from 10 cm cubes (1U). Universities build them, and NASA's CubeSat Launch Initiative gives selected ones a ride to space at no cost.

iss.name: ISS
iss.text: The International Space Station flies at about 420 km. Small satellites go up to it as cargo and are released from it.

budget.name: Budget, k
budget.text: Game credits in thousands: parts, the ride to orbit and ground stations all cost money.

orbit.name: Orbit
orbit.text: The path around the Earth. Its height sets the speed: at 415 km one orbit takes about 93 minutes.

inclination.name: Inclination
inclination.text: The angle between the orbit and the equator. The ISS orbit is tilted 51.6°, so the satellite flies over most inhabited places.

shadow.name: Earth's shadow
shadow.text: Part of every orbit is spent in the shadow of the Earth. The solar panels give nothing there, so the battery must last until sunlight.

groundStation.name: Ground station
groundStation.text: An antenna on Earth that talks to the satellite while it is in view — a few minutes per pass. Its band must match your radio.

margin.name: Margin
margin.text: Spare capacity kept on purpose. NASA asks for at least 15% extra mass at the concept stage, because designs always grow.

slots.name: Slots
slots.text: Places for parts inside the bus. A small bus has 6.

uhf.name: UHF radio
uhf.text: A simple, slow radio (38.4 kbit/s). Enough for a magnetometer; a camera would need a faster band such as S or X.

drag.name: Atmospheric drag
drag.text: Even very thin air slows a satellite down. It loses height, and below about 180 km it burns up.

groundTrack.name: Ground track
groundTrack.text: The line on the map under the satellite. The Earth turns beneath the orbit, so every pass is shifted west.

contact.name: Contact
contact.text: The minutes when a station sees the satellite. Data goes down only then.

bottleneck.name: Bottleneck
bottleneck.text: The resource with the smallest margin. Improving it helps the most.

segment.name: Segments
segment.text: NASA splits a mission into launch, space, ground and user segments. One weak segment fails the whole mission.

seed.name: Seed
seed.text: A number that fixes the random events. The same design and seed give the same flight.

iss.plannerHint: A launch site above 51.6° latitude needs a plane change. From a lower insertion orbit the ship catches up with the station faster but needs more Δv to climb. The relay keeps the ship in contact all the time.
iss.cargoTotal: Loaded {{loaded}} of {{goal}} kg · science {{science}}% (need at least {{min}}%)

rendezvous.title: Rendezvous with the ISS

explain.phasing: On the lower orbit the ship flies faster and gains on the station every orbit.
explain.transfer: The first burn lifts the far side of the orbit up to the station; the second makes the orbit round there.
explain.approach: The last metres: a slow approach and waiting for a contact with the ground.
explain.docked: The cargo is on board the station.
explain.missed: The ship ran out of propellant or time before docking.
